editions.title: Trump, Xi and Putin set to meet as Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
editions.notification: Trump, Xi and Putin are set for a first three-way nuclear meeting in Shenzhen, as Ukraine cuts Crimea's road link.
editions.intro:
Attention in Shenzhen is on the first in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, due on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The White House has confirmed the trilateral, which is expected to focus on nuclear arms control after New START expired in February, though China has not formally confirmed it and Moscow says the format is not yet agreed. A senior US official said no agreement is expected. Trump has left the summit early, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent representing the US at some sessions. Beijing has called the meeting groundbreaking, while critics describe it as a "New Yalta" moment.

The wider conflict is adding pressure. Iran has fired drones and missiles at US sites in Bahrain and Kuwait after American strikes, and a Hormuz tanker fire has put a US-Iran memorandum at risk. Ukraine has partly collapsed the Crimean Bridge, and a third attack reportedly hit it on the same week. Separately, Nvidia has posted record revenue under interim chief Colette Kress, but its board has ruled out Jensen Huang's return, and Washington has widened AI chip export curbs, with Congress now moving to tighten them further.

Markets are dealing with several strands at once. Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 a share, making it the largest stock-market debut on record, with trading on the Nasdaq due on Thursday. Gold has fallen to its weakest level since September 2025 as markets price a possible US rate rise, and Deutsche Bank has fallen sharply after a leak of internal records. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign an EU food and farming reset at a Friday summit, which he says shows Brexit "has not worked".

editions.title: Trump, Xi and Putin set for Shenzhen summit as Iran fight widens
editions.notification: Trump, Xi and Putin are set to meet in Shenzhen, as Iran strikes reach Kuwait and Bahrain and Nvidia's Huang fallout deepens.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is the first planned in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, set for Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The White House has confirmed it, though China and the Kremlin have not fully done so, and no agreement is expected. Nuclear arms control is the main agenda item, following the expiry of New START in February. The meeting is being overshadowed by escalation in the Gulf. Iran has fired drones and missiles at US facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait after American strikes, and Qeshm Island was reportedly hit. Most projectiles were intercepted, but the attacks threaten the US-Iran memorandum that opened a 60-day negotiating window.

Alongside the summit, US export policy is tightening. Washington has required licences for advanced chip exports to five more countries and closed a loophole allowing remote access to Chinese computing power, while the Justice Department confirmed a criminal probe into Megaspeed. Nvidia's position is at the centre of this. It posted record revenue of $115.8bn, but its board has ruled out bringing back Jensen Huang, who resigned over an affair with a woman US officials suspect of Chinese intelligence links. Congress is moving on chip export bills, and Nvidia shares remain about 30% below their record high.

Elsewhere, Ukraine's strike on the Kerch bridge and the Crimean Bridge has cut a key supply route for Russia, timed ahead of the Shenzhen meeting. Oil prices are sensitive to the Gulf and Red Sea, where Houthis now control Bab al-Mandab. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to sign an EU reset deal in Brussels on Friday.

editions.notification: Nvidia's leadership crisis deepens as US chip curbs tighten and Trump heads to a historic Shenzhen summit.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's leadership crisis remains the day's biggest story, and it is now spilling into policy and markets. Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence has prompted fresh reporting on his wife's links to Chinese state-backed businesses, a New York Times account of his daughter Madison's influence, and talk of a return campaign backed by Elon Musk. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the company reports its first results without Huang on 17 November. Meanwhile the US has widened AI chip export licensing to five more countries and closed a remote-access loophole, while Congress moves towards tighter rules, and Washington's own cabinet is openly divided over how hard to press Beijing.

The wider backdrop is a sharp tech sell-off. Intel plunged after a weak forecast, Alphabet had its worst day on record, and Nasdaq futures fell as investors demanded proof of returns on AI spending. Asian chip stocks slid again, and the ECB and Anthropic's large Nasdaq listing have added to fears of an AI repricing. Anthropic is set to list this week, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks on AI scenarios come as markets price a likely December rate rise.

Geopolitics is equally heavy. US strikes on southern Iran have triggered attacks on US bases across the Gulf for a seventh night, and US intelligence reportedly puts Iran's missile stock at up to 2,500, undermining administration claims. Houthis now control the Bab al-Mandab Strait after Saudi-backed forces withdrew, pushing oil higher. Trump, Xi and Putin are due to meet at APEC in Shenzhen on Thursday, the first in-person trilateral, though no agreement is expected.

editions.title: Iran strikes spread as Nvidia's Huang fallout and Xi-Putin-Trump summit loom
editions.notification: US-Iran strikes enter a seventh night, Nvidia's leadership crisis deepens, and a first Xi-Putin-Trump summit is set.
editions.intro:
The conflict with Iran is the lead story again, now in its seventh consecutive night of strikes. Iranian missiles and drones have targeted US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait, and reports say at least five people died in a strike on a wedding in Kuhestak. Kuwait suspended operations at its international airport, and Iran's energy ministry asked citizens to cut power use after strikes on the grid. Separately, reports say the Trump administration warned Gulf allies that hostilities could resume as soon as Wednesday. Figures from both sides are unverified, and the White House has not confirmed any timing.

The second thread is Nvidia. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, after reports of affairs including one with a Singapore-based executive US officials say was recruited by Chinese intelligence, has wiped roughly $600bn from the company's value in a week. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the first results without Huang are due on 17 November. Lawmakers are pressing for testimony, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under scrutiny, and Huang reportedly discussed a return. Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup".

Diplomacy and markets are tied to both. A first in-person Xi-Trump-Putin meeting is set for Shenzhen during APEC, with nuclear arms on the agenda. Anthropic's IPO, priced at up to $1.4tn, is due to price on 18 November. Oil is elevated, with Brent near $94 to $96, and the Fed is signalling possible rate rises, which pushed the dollar to a 19-month high.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang fallout deepens as Iran strikes widen
editions.notification: Huang's exit is rattling Nvidia and Congress, while US-Iran strikes enter a seventh night. Here's where things stand.
editions.intro:
Nvidia remains the day's dominant story, though the focus has shifted from Jensen Huang's resignation to what happens next. Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress, with Senate and House committees seeking closed-door interviews on 1 to 3 December. Pressure is building on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is accused of stalling action against Megaspeed, the Singapore firm linked to Alice Huang. Nvidia has lost roughly $550bn in five days, and its first results without Huang are due on 17 November. A petition with more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, now asks the board to reinstate him.

The biggest geopolitical story is the widening US-Iran conflict. A seventh consecutive night of American strikes has prompted Iranian missile and drone attacks on US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait, with reports of civilian deaths in Kuhestak. Two oil tankers were reportedly hit by mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and crude prices rose. Diplomacy is also moving: the White House confirmed a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 19 November, though no agreement is expected and Ukraine is not on the agenda. Europe has chosen five national security advisers to represent it in future talks, while Moscow's reported demands on Nato and Britain set a hard starting point.

Markets were under broader pressure. US Treasuries had their worst week since the 2025 tariff announcement after higher-than-expected inflation, and Fed officials signal rate rises. Bitcoin fell to a three-month low near $63,000, and Anthropic's Nasdaq listing, priced at up to about $1.4tn, is set for 18 November. FAA disruption from a copper-to-fibre upgrade failure left about 1.5 million travellers affected, with normal operations expected before Thanksgiving.

editions.title: Huang exit rattles Nvidia as Trump's Xi-Putin meeting is set
editions.notification: Nvidia shares slide after Jensen Huang quits as CEO; Colette Kress steps in as interim chief.
editions.intro:
Nvidia dominated the day after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, president and board member following reports of extramarital affairs, one reportedly involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The shares closed down just over 4% on Friday after falling as much as 14% in morning trading, and the stock has lost close to $1 trillion this month. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, Harvey Jones is the new independent chair, and the board has reportedly approached Arm's Rene Haas about the permanent role. The political fallout is spreading to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is accused of stalling action against Singapore's Megaspeed, and Democrats and Republicans are seeking answers.

Elsewhere, the White House confirmed that Donald Trump will meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, expected on 19 November, though a senior US official said no agreement is expected. Putin, meanwhile, signalled no compromise on Ukraine after meeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow. Europe agreed a five-nation group to speak for it in future talks.

Markets were also shaken by a global Microsoft 365 outage and a rare nationwide FAA ground stop that cancelled more than 6,700 US flights. On energy, the IEA says global oil supply has returned to surplus for the first time since the Iran war began, while Iran says two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

It is the largest stock-market debut on record, eclipsing SpaceX's $75bn earlier this year, and values the Claude maker at roughly $1.5tn fully diluted. Shares start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading. Including a $26bn private placement bought by strategic partners such as Google and Nvidia, total deal size reaches about $107.3bn.

The debut is being read as a test of appetite for AI valuations and of OpenAI's expected listing, at a time when the Federal Reserve is openly debating whether AI spending poses financial-stability risks. Nvidia remains the main US story. Its board has ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, even after third-quarter revenue of $115.8bn beat forecasts, leaving interim chief executive Colette Kress to run the company.

Elsewhere, Washington widened AI chip export licensing to five more countries, and the US Treasury 10-year yield has reportedly topped 5%, a level that raises borrowing costs across the economy.

Nvidia is the common thread. Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: Washington moves to tighten AI chip exports to China
Tech.notification: Congress is closing in on tougher AI chip export rules for China, with a law possible by year-end
Tech.summary:
Tighter controls on AI chips bound for China dominate the tech agenda. Bipartisan momentum in Washington is building for new export limits, with a possible law by the end of the year. The push follows the Huang affair and reports that Nvidia sold $4 billion of chips to Singapore firm Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting them to China and is under Justice Department investigation.

The curbs are already reaching Chinese tech giants. A Commerce Department rule announced on Monday stops Chinese firms from remotely using cutting-edge Nvidia chips in data centres abroad, and Tencent has conceded that it will slow its AI model training in the short run. Alibaba, whose Hong Kong shares have fallen nine days in a row, faces the same pressure ahead of its results on Thursday.

Nvidia is the common thread. Jensen Huang's resignation has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off its value, and its private-company stakes now stand at $65.5bn, which raises doubts about how much venture money it will keep putting into startups. Meanwhile, Anthropic's listing this week is set to be one of the largest flotations ever.

Finance.title: Anthropic prices record $81bn IPO at $83 a share
Finance.notification: Anthropic prices record $81bn IPO above range, valuing it near $1.5tn. Trading starts Thursday on Nasdaq.
Finance.summary:
Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its original $70 to $78 range, raising about $81.3bn including secondary sales. It is the largest stock-market debut on record, eclipsing SpaceX's $75bn earlier this year, and values the Claude maker at roughly $1.5tn fully diluted. Shares start trading on Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading. Including a $26bn private placement bought by strategic partners such as Google and Nvidia, total deal size reaches about $107.3bn.

The debut is being read as a test of appetite for AI valuations and of OpenAI's expected listing, at a time when the Federal Reserve is openly debating whether AI spending poses financial-stability risks. Nvidia remains the main US story. Its board has ruled out reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, even after third-quarter revenue of $115.8bn beat forecasts, leaving interim chief executive Colette Kress to run the company.

Elsewhere, Washington widened AI chip export licensing to five more countries, and the US Treasury 10-year yield has reportedly topped 5%, a level that raises borrowing costs across the economy.

World.title: Ukraine cuts Crimean Bridge as Trump, Xi and Putin meet
World.notification: Ukraine says the Crimean Bridge road span is out of action, as Trump, Xi and Putin prepare for talks in Shenzhen.
World.summary:
Ukraine has badly damaged the Crimean Bridge, with a large arch of the road span reportedly falling into the Kerch Strait and cutting the peninsula's direct road link to Russia. Kyiv calls it a weeks-long operation, and the Kremlin says the bridge will be restored. The strike lands just before the first in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where nuclear arms control is expected to dominate and Ukraine is reportedly not on the agenda.

The US story is also heavy. Overall the US is contending with a run of digital outages, with officials rejecting a cyberattack link, while Rubio and Mullin dismiss the AI theory. Washington has lost its measles elimination status, and Iran's missile stockpile is in question after a US intelligence estimate contradicted White House claims. Markets are watching oil, which rose on Red Sea and Hormuz risks, and gold, which fell to a one-year low as traders priced a possible December Fed rate rise.

In the UK, the government is set to scrap most new leasehold homes and cap ground rent, while Andy Burnham is signalling a slower Brexit reset ahead of a Friday EU summit. In Europe, Deutsche Bank faces a German data inquiry after a major leak, and Ukraine's backers meet in Berlin. Asia's main story is the Shenzhen summit itself, with South Korea's tax exam cheating scandal adding a domestic twist.

Fashion.title: Luxury shares slip as AI selloff stokes spending fears
Fashion.notification: European luxury stocks slide as AI-driven market jitters raise doubts over wealthy US spending
Fashion.summary:
European luxury shares fell about 2% on Tuesday, with Hermès down more than 4% and Moncler at a four-year low after a Morgan Stanley downgrade. Investors fear a renewed AI-related selloff could erode the wealth of American consumers, one of the sector's few remaining growth drivers, on top of weak Chinese demand and disappointing third-quarter sales.

Sportswear is also under pressure. Nike shares fell 6.3% after its first investor day in nine years, where management set a fiscal 2031 plan with $5 billion of revenue growth. Analysts were split, with Jefferies calling it a credible floor while Truist and BNP Paribas noted that gains are back-loaded.

Elsewhere, the sector's longer-term outlook is more measured. Bain and Altagamma see the luxury market growing from €1.52 trillion in 2026 to between €2.2 and €2.6 trillion by 2035, though mainland China is forecast to decline. Brands keep investing in China regardless, with Gucci picking Shanghai for a May 2027 cruise show.
